body:
Australia accounted for two of the three Asia-Pacific investments in Federated Hermes’ latest co-investment fund, as the global investment firm saw opportunities in the country’s lower mid-market.

“We’re a global firm. We source around 800 investable co-investment opportunities a year, and we’ll probably invest in about 20,” Brooks Harrington, CIO private equity at Federated Hermes told Investor Daily .

The fund’s seed portfolio had 14 investments, three of which came from Asia-Pacific, including two from Australia.

“So, literally, two-thirds of our private equity activity in Asia-Pacific over the last year and a half or so has been in Australia,” he said.

Harrington said Australia’s language alignment and regulatory structure were among the attractions, alongside its position as an ally of the US, and pointed to the country’s market for founders selling businesses, succession processes and corporate carve-outs.

“We think the lower end of the market—between $100 million and $250 million—is a solid area in which to deploy capital, and that’s where we’re seeing opportunities,” he said.

The lower mid-market also offered a broader pool of potential investments, Harrington said. He described the segment as companies with enterprise values generally below $500 million, while noting that the fund’s current portfolio had a median enterprise value of about $90 million.

The firm was the first institutional investor in about 40 per cent of the 14 companies in the portfolio.

Harrington said this position could give investors scope to work with founders on professionalising a business, including developing management, sales, go-to-market and finance functions.

“The value created through those operational improvements can accrue to the buyer,” he said.

That approach contrasted with larger-market deals, where companies may have already received institutional investment and operational changes.

Harrington said the lower end of the market had attracted about 10 per cent of private equity capital while representing 90 per cent of the investable universe.

“I’ve seen a statistic that 60 per cent of the capital raised in the last 12 months went to just 12 firms,” he said.

Strong brands and access to wealth-channel investors helped direct capital towards established managers, he added, leaving the middle and upper market more crowded.

Harrington said larger transactions could also be harder to complete because they required more debt, making them more exposed to higher interest rates and unfavourable capital markets.

Selling larger companies could be difficult when the IPO window was effectively shut, although there had been a few exceptions. By comparison, smaller companies could be grown before a sale and sold to a wider pool of buyers, including strategic acquirers and private equity funds.

Harrington said a business bought at a $90 million valuation could potentially reach about $300 million after five years of revenue and earnings growth and professionalisation, a level at which those buyers could acquire it.

Federated Hermes recorded about 15 exits across its portfolio in the previous 12 months, Harrington said: seven to strategic buyers, seven to private equity funds and one through an IPO.

The exit figures were relevant as investors increasingly focused on distributions to paid-in capital, or DPI, and asked where future exits would come from.

Harrington said about 40 per cent of private equity-backed companies were more than seven years old, and there were 38,000 such companies stating that portfolios needed a clear exit path, particularly as private equity had about US$1.3 trillion in dry powder still to invest.

The lower mid-market opportunity came with its own risks, including less experienced management teams and the costs of filling gaps in a company’s leadership.

Harrington said investors needed to assess which roles a business would require, whether the existing team was suited to its next stage and whether the cost of changes had been included in financial projections.

He also argued that emerging managers were not necessarily riskier than established firms.

Harrington said some new managers had lengthy private equity careers, strong references and track records from larger firms, but limited bandwidth and perceived risk could make it harder for investors to back them.

“LPs like to invest in funds with well-known brands,” he said. “Those funds are perceived as less risky and are easier to get approved internally.”

Harrington said investors in lower-market funds often needed to monitor more managers and deals, and to investigate how much of a track record belonged to an individual rather than their former firm.

That extra work could make it easier for limited partners to commit to established funds with longer histories.

Looking ahead, Harrington said institutional investors in the US and elsewhere were relatively fully allocated, with new capital coming from the wealth channel. He expected slower industry growth and said exits would not clear in a neat, orderly way, leaving secondary markets with a significant role.

“We’re operating on the assumption that this is the new normal,” he said. The firm was seeking lower mid-market companies with healthy growth rates that would remain attractive to buyers several years after acquisition.
